q: Which ancient Greek poet is traditionally credited with composing both the Iliad and the Odyssey?
note: Scholars still argue over whether Homer was one person, several, or a tradition of oral performers.

q: Which American author wrote Little Women, about the four March sisters?
note: Alcott drew the sisters from her own family in Concord, Massachusetts, and wrote the book in a few weeks at her publisher's nagging.

q: Which author created the man-cub Mowgli in The Jungle Book?
note: Kipling was born in Bombay and wrote the stories while living in Vermont.

q: Which Scottish author wrote both Treasure Island and Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde?
note: Chronically ill for most of his life, he spent his final years in Samoa, where he is buried.

q: In Greek mythology, what is the name of the three-headed dog that guards the entrance to the underworld?
note: Dante borrowed him for the Inferno, setting him to guard the circle of the gluttons.

q: In Greek myth, which king was granted a wish that turned everything he touched to gold?
note: In a separate tale Midas judges a music contest against Apollo and is given donkey's ears for his poor taste.

q: In Greek myth, which beautiful youth wasted away after falling in love with his own reflection in a pool?
note: The nymph Echo, who loved him, had already been reduced to repeating other people's words.

q: In Greek myth, how many Labours was Heracles made to perform as a penance?
note: They were set by his cousin King Eurystheus, and the first was to kill the Nemean Lion.

q: Which vast temple complex, built in the 12th century, appears on the national flag of Cambodia?
note: It is the only building that appears on any country’s national flag.

q: "Dr. Seuss" was the pen name of which American writer and illustrator?
note: Seuss was his mother's maiden name, and he was not a doctor of anything.

q: The Victorian novelist who published Middlemarch and Silas Marner as "George Eliot" was really a woman with what name?
note: She chose a male pen name partly to escape the era's assumption that women wrote only light romances.

q: Agatha Christie's moustachioed detective Hercule Poirot is of which nationality, often wrongly assumed to be French?
note: When Christie killed him off in Curtain, Poirot received a front-page obituary in The New York Times.

q: In L. Frank Baum's original novel The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, what colour are Dorothy's magic slippers?
note: The ruby slippers were an invention of the 1939 MGM film, which wanted a colour that would pop in Technicolor.

q: In Greek myth, the Titan Atlas was condemned to hold up what on his shoulders?
note: The Roman statue known as the Farnese Atlas shows him carrying a celestial sphere, not the Earth.

q: At the Palace of Westminster in London, what exactly is "Big Ben" the name of?
note: The tower that houses it was simply the Clock Tower until it was renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012.

q: Which was completed first, the Statue of Liberty or the Eiffel Tower?
note: Gustave Eiffel designed the statue's internal iron framework three years before his tower opened.

q: Which was published first, Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea or H.G. Wells's The Time Machine?
a: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea
note: The leagues in Verne's title measure how far the Nautilus travels, not how deep it goes.

q: Which Austrian painter covered The Kiss in gold leaf during his so-called Golden Phase?
note: The painting hangs in the Belvedere in Vienna, where it has become the city's unofficial emblem.

q: Which American abstract painter made his best-known works by dripping and flinging paint onto canvases laid on the floor?
note: A 1956 Time magazine piece nicknamed him "Jack the Dripper".

q: In Greek myth, who was punished in the underworld by having to roll a boulder uphill, only for it to roll back down forever?
note: Albert Camus made him the hero of a famous essay, arguing that we must imagine him happy.

q: In Roman legend, which twin brothers were suckled by a she-wolf before one of them founded Rome?
note: The twins quarrelled over the new city's walls, and Romulus killed his brother.

q: In which city does Hagia Sophia stand, raised as a cathedral in the 6th century under the emperor Justinian?
note: It served as a cathedral for some 900 years, then as a mosque for nearly 500.

q: The musical My Fair Lady is based on which George Bernard Shaw play about a phonetics professor and a flower girl?
note: Shaw won an Academy Award for the screenplay of the 1938 film version of his own play.

q: Which American author wrote Beloved, about a formerly enslaved woman haunted by the daughter she killed?
note: In 1993 she became the first Black woman awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.

q: The painting everyone calls "Whistler's Mother" was actually titled by the artist as an arrangement in which two colours?
accept: Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1
note: France bought it in 1891, and it hangs today in the Musee d'Orsay rather than anywhere in America.

q: Which was published first, C.S. Lewis's The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe or Tolkien's The Fellowship of the Ring?
a: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe
accept: The Lion the Witch and the Wardrobe
note: Narnia beat Frodo to print by nearly four years, though Tolkien's The Hobbit had appeared back in 1937.

q: "Lewis Carroll" was the pen name of which Oxford mathematics lecturer?
note: He built the pen name by Latinising his first two names and then swapping them round.

q: Victor Hugo's novel about the bell-ringer Quasimodo was published in French under what title, which is the name of a building rather than a person?
note: The book's popularity helped shame France into restoring the then-crumbling cathedral.

q: Which Renaissance architect designed and built the vast brick dome of Florence Cathedral?
note: Finished in 1436, it is still the largest masonry dome ever built.

q: Which Belgian Surrealist painted a careful picture of a pipe captioned "This is not a pipe"?
note: He also produced the bowler-hatted man with a green apple for a face, The Son of Man.
